content.title: The Artemis II mission
content.text: Humanity's return to the MoonNASA's Artemis II mission sent the first humans back to the Moon in over 50 years. A crew of four astronauts undertook a 10-day mission around the Moon and back, kicking off the first crewed mission of the agency's Artemis program, which aims to land people on the Moon in 2028 and eventually set up a base there. Latest UpdatesApril 10, 2026 · 6:37 p.m. PTThe Artemis II crew has left the Orion CapsuleAfter completing medical assessments, all four Artemis II crew members exited the Orion Capsule, with assistance from U.S. Navy personnel.April 10, 2026 · 5:07 p.m. PTSplashdown successful! The Orion capsule carrying the Artemis II crew successfully splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.April 10, 2026 · 6:05 a.m. PTArtemis II will return to Earth today To conclude a very successful mission, the Orion spacecraft carrying the Artemis II crew will splash down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego at 8:07 p.m. ET today. Here is the timeline of events (all times in ET):7:33 p.m.: Orion’s crew module will separate from the service module, exposing its heat shield for the spacecraft’s return through Earth’s atmosphere, where it will encounter temperatures of about 1,650 degrees Celsius (3,000 degrees Fahrenheit).7:37 p.m.: Following separation, Orion will perform an 18-second crew module raise burn beginning to set the proper entry angle and align the heat shield for atmospheric interface.7:53 p.m.: The spacecraft makes first contact with the upper atmosphere, about 122,000 meters (400,000 feet) above Earth’s surface. It will be traveling nearly 35 times the speed of sound, and the crew is expected to experience up to 3.9 Gs. This marks the start of a planned 6-minute communications blackout as plasma builds around the capsule.8:03 p.m.: At around 67,000 meters (22,000 feet) in altitude, the drogue parachutes will deploy, slowing and stabilizing the capsule as Orion nears splashdown.8:04 p.m.: At around 1,800 meters (6,000 feet), the drogues will release, and the three main parachutes will deploy, reducing Orion’s speed to less than 219 kilometers per hour (136 miles per hour).8:07 p.m.: Slowing to 32 kilometers per hour (20 miles per hour), Orion will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, completing the Artemis II crew’s return to Earth and a 1,117,659-kilometer (694,481-mile) journey.Within two hours after splashdown, recovery teams will retrieve the crew from Orion, assist them onto an inflatable raft, and then use helicopters to deliver them to a nearby ship. Once aboard, the astronauts will undergo post‑mission medical evaluations before returning to shore, where awaiting aircraft will take them to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.April 7, 2026 · 7:00 a.m. PTLunar flyby images have arrived Browse the images taken by the Artemis II crew during lunar flyby and the total solar eclipse here.April 6, 2026 · 6:35 p.m. PTThe Artemis II crew is heading homeThe Artemis II crew has completed the mission’s lunar observation period and is now beginning the return trip back to Earth. Here's what will happen in the coming days:April 7-9: Orion performs three trajectory corrections to fine-tune its return to Earth. On day 7, the crew rests off-duty, and on day 8, the crew demonstrates the construction of a radiation shelter construction demo and performs manual piloting tests.April 10: The crew dons spacesuits and compression garments to prepare for reentry. About 122,000 meters (400,000 feet) above Earth, Orion's service module separates from the crew module, and Orion reenters Earth's atmosphere at 40,000 kilometers per hour (25,000 miles per hour). Two drogue parachutes slow Orion to roughly 480 kilometers per hour (300 miles per hour). Then, three pilot parachutes, followed by three main parachutes, slow the capsule to 27 kilometers per hour (17 miles per hour). Artemis II splashes down off the coast of San Diego, California.April 6, 2026 · 6:30 p.m. PTOrion is in the darkest part of the Moon's shadowThe crew is observing the darkness of the Moon, the stars beyond, and some visible planets — truly awesome sights.Victor Glover said, "There are stars… An unreal view… The moon in the foreground is one of the darkest things we see out the window. And now, deep space behind it is kind of dark blue, like it looks from Earth, but we can also still see stars. It’s quite a wicked view."Commander Reid Wiseman added, "It’s just indescribable. No matter how long we look at this, our brains are not processing this image in front of us. It is absolutely spectacular, surreal. There’s no… there’s no adjectives. I’m going to need to invent some new ones to describe what we are looking at out this window."April 6, 2026 · 5:36 p.m. PTA solar eclipse in spaceThe Sun has disappeared behind the Moon from the perspective of the crew aboard Orion. Although this is a total solar eclipse, it will not look like the ones we see on Earth since the Moon will appear much larger. It will give the Artemis II astronauts a chance to study the Sun's corona (its outer atmosphere) as it passes behind the Moon. During the eclipse, they may also be able to observe lunar dust that is illuminated by the Sun, as well as flashes of light from meteoroids striking the Moon's surface.The Sun will reappear at 9:32 p.m. ET., giving the crew nearly an hour of eclipse observation.April 6, 2026 · 4:25 p.m. PTMission control has regained contact with Orion The Orion spacecraft has emerged from behind the Moon, resuming communication between the Artemis II crew and mission control. April 6, 2026 · 4:02 p.m. PTOrion reaches maximum distance from EarthThe Orion spacecraft has reached its maximum distance from Earth at 406,771 kilometers (252,756 miles), setting a new record for human spaceflight. April 6, 2026 · 4:00 p.m. PTOrion reaches closest point to the MoonOrion has reached its closest approach to the Moon at about 6,545 kilometers (4,067 miles) above the lunar surface. At this point, the spacecraft is traveling at about 97,949 kilometers per hour (60,863 miles per hour) relative to Earth, but only 5,052 kilometers per hour (3,139 miles per hour) relative to the Moon. April 6, 2026 · 3:22 p.m. PTOrion is approaching its close passOrion will soon pass around the Moon, at which time mission control will temporarily lose communication with the spacecraft. During this 40-minute period, the following milestones will occur (times in ET):6:45 p.m.: During “Earthset,” Earth will glide behind the Moon from Orion’s perspective.7:02 p.m.: Orion reaches its closest approach to the Moon at 4,070 miles above the surface.7:07 p.m.: Crew reach their maximum distance from Earth during the mission (252,706 miles).7:25 p.m.: “Earthrise” marks Earth coming back into view on the opposite edge of the Moon. 7:25 p.m.: Mission control will re-acquire communication with the astronauts. April 6, 2026 · 11:45 a.m. PTThe lunar observation period has begunThe Orion spacecraft is now close enough to the Moon for the crew and science team to make impactful science observations. This observation period, which includes the lunar flyby, is expected to last about seven hours.April 6, 2026 · 11:00 a.m. PTArtemis II has broken a distance recordThe Orion capsule has officially traveled farther from Earth than any previous crewed mission, surpassing the record of 400,171 kilometers (248,655 miles) set by Apollo 13 in 1970. The reason Artemis II broke this record before even reaching the Moon is because of the Moon's elliptical orbit around Earth. Right now, the Moon is farther from Earth than it was during Apollo missions.April 6, 2026 · 8:30 a.m. PTLunar flyby to take place today The Orion spacecraft will carry the Artemis II crew around the farside of the Moon today. Here are the key milestones expected (all times in ET):1:30 p.m.: The science officer in the Mission Control Center at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston will brief the crew on their science goals for the upcoming flyby. 1:56 p.m.: The Artemis II crew is expected to surpass the record previously set by the Apollo 13 crew in 1970 for the farthest humans have ever traveled from Earth.2:45 p.m.: Lunar observations begin. 6:44 p.m.: Mission control expects to temporarily lose communication with the crew as the Orion spacecraft passes behind the Moon.6:45 p.m.: During “Earthset,” Earth will glide behind the Moon from Orion’s perspective.7:02 p.m.: Orion reaches its closest approach to the Moon at 4,070 miles above the surface.7:07 p.m.: Crew reach their maximum distance from Earth during the mission (252,706 miles).7:25 p.m.: “Earthrise” marks Earth coming back into view on the opposite edge of the Moon. 7:25 p.m.: Mission control will re-acquire communication with the astronauts.8:35-9:32 p.m.: During a solar eclipse, the Sun will pass behind the Moon from the crew’s perspective.9:20 p.m.: Lunar observations conclude. April 2, 2026 · 4:57 p.m. PTTranslunar injection burn completeThe spacecraft has completed the translunar injection burn, accelerating Orion to escape velocity and sending the crew toward the Moon on their free-return trajectory.April 2, 2026 · 8:58 a.m. PTWhat's keeping the Artemis II astronauts safe?April 2, 2026 · 6:15 a.m. PTThe perigee raise burn is complete The spacecraft's main engine completed a 43-second burn to raise the lowest point (or perigee) of its orbit and refine its trajectory, placing it in a stable high-Earth orbit that aligns with its path to the Moon.April 1, 2026 · 3:37 p.m. PTWe have liftoff!Artemis II has successfully launched! The Space Launch System rocket took off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 6:35 p.m. ET, launching astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen aboard the Orion capsule on a trajectory that will take them around the Moon and back to Earth.April 1, 2026 · 3:26 p.m. PTLiftoff is scheduled for 6:35:12 p.m. ETThe countdown has begun toward a liftoff at 6:35:12 p.m. ETApril 1, 2026 · 3:21 p.m. PTWe are GO for launchThe Artemis II launch has passed all checks and is ready to proceed with the launch countdown.April 1, 2026 · 2:59 p.m. PTBattery issue will not delay launchNASA has reported that the LAS battery issue is believed to be an instrumentation issue and will not affect today’s launch.The weather has also continued to improve and has now been upgraded to 90% go for launch.April 1, 2026 · 2:51 p.m. PTLaunch timeline on trackThe final poll of the launch team, checking whether each component is GO for launch, will take place in around 15-20 minutes, at T-16m. The launch team is on track to launch toward the beginning of the launch window. April 1, 2026 · 2:36 p.m. PTWhite room detachmentThe white room, from which the Artemis II crew entered the Orion capsule, has now been detached from the capsule. April 1, 2026 · 2:33 p.m. PTLAS battery temperature issueThe launch team is reporting an issue with a battery on the launch abort system. The temperature for one of the two LAS batteries is out of its normal range. This may be a sensor issue or a problem with the battery itself. This needs to be addressed before launch. The team is working on troubleshooting the issue. April 1, 2026 · 2:18 p.m. PTTechnicians have completed the launch abort system hatch closureThe closeout team has verified hatch alignment, engaged locking mechanisms, and confirmed pressure integrity. This step ensures that the Orion spacecraft is fully sealed and ready for flight. The launch abort system hatch is designed to safeguard astronauts during the flight path and, if necessary, enable a rapid escape in the event of an emergency. April 1, 2026 · 2:14 p.m. PTLaunch weather update: "Seeing some good sunlight now"Though there is still a bit of poor weather near the launchpad, NASA forecasts those clouds will move farther away. Clearer skies appear to be coming in from the west. April 1, 2026 · 2:10 p.m. PTRange is GOThe range has verified its flight termination system and is reporting that the issue is fixed, and the launch has clearance from that team. April 1, 2026 · 1:31 p.m. PTFlight termination system issueThe launch team has been made aware of an issue relating to the flight termination system. This system sends a signal to the rocket if it starts to veer off path. The issue is at the flight range facility, not on the rocket. The range team is working to address this issue with assistance from the launch team. This is not currently causing a countdown pause. April 1, 2026 · 12:43 p.m. PTNo constraints to launchNASA has announced that there are currently no major constraints to today's planned launch. This includes weather conditions, the rocket and capsule, the crew, and all other key factors. April 1, 2026 · 12:12 p.m. PTThe European Service Module Credit: ESAThe Artemis II crew will depend on Orion's service module for power, consumables (water, air, etc), and thrust. But unlike the Apollo era, which was a U.S.-only program, the service module is provided by the European Space Agency (ESA). It's a design that leverages hardware developed for their cargo transport module used for the International Space Station.The European Service Module deal was signed in January of 2013, not long after Congress mandated the construction of the SLS and continuation of Orion. NASA was facing severe budgetary strain, including a 10% across-the-board cut imposed to nearly all federal agencies.The deal provided NASA with a service module for Orion, saving the agency billions of dollars. In turn, NASA counted Orion service modules as ESA fulfilling its financial obligation to the space station. There are no alternatives to the ESM. Every mission to the Moon in Orion will, by default, be an international partnership.April 1, 2026 · 11:58 a.m. PTThe crew is on board OrionThe astronauts are aboard the spacecraft and carrying out checks.April 1, 2026 · 11:18 a.m. PTArtemis II crew arrives at LC-39B Credit: NASAFor the first time in 20 years, astronauts are walking onto launch complex 39B to board a rocket to space.April 1, 2026 · 10:49 a.m. PTNASA's Artemis II crew walkout is underwayArtemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen have begun their trip to Launchpad Complex 39B at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.April 1, 2026 · 9:00 a.m. PTThe SLS rocket is being fueledFollow NASA's feed for more up-to-the-minute details about launch preparations. The Moon from Orion's window The Artemis II crew took this photo of the Moon through the window of the Orion spacecraft at the tail end of the fifth day of their mission. At this time, the Moon's gravity had begun to exert a stronger pull on the spacecraft than Earth's.Image: NASAArtemis II was a test flight, meaning that its primary objective was to demonstrate key systems that would be needed for a crewed mission to land on the Moon. That includes Artemis II's launch vehicle, the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket, and its crew capsule, Orion.The mission took about 10 days to complete. The mission launched from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on April 1, using Launch Complex 39B — the same historic pad used for Apollo and Space Shuttle missions. Orion orbited Earth twice while the crew tested out its systems, then the mission headed for the Moon, flying as close as 8,000 kilometers (5,000 miles) from its surface on April 6. After traveling back to Earth, the crew reentered the atmosphere, descended under parachutes, and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on April 10. Artemis II map Artemis II will be the first crewed flight of NASA’s deep space exploration system, featuring the Orion spacecraft, the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket, and ground systems at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Over roughly 10 days in deep space, four astronauts will test Orion’s systems in their intended environment, paving the way for the Artemis III mission to return humans to the Moon.Image: NASAThe crew Four astronauts were selected for NASA’s Artemis II mission: Commander Reid Wiseman (NASA), pilot Victor Glover (NASA), mission specialist Christina Koch (NASA), and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen (Canadian Space Agency). Reid Wiseman is a native of Cockeysville, Maryland. He first gained an interest in spaceflight seeing fighters jets fly overhead and, one time, the Space Shuttle on the back of its 747 transport plane. After earning his Master's degree in systems engineering from Johns Hopkins University, Wiseman became a Navy test pilot and ultimately a captain in the navy. He was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2009, flew on an expedition to the International Space Station in 2014, and served as chief of NASA's Astronaut Office from 2020-2022.Christina Koch is a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, and has wanted to be an astronaut since she was five years old. After earning a bachelors and a master's degree in electrical engineering from North Carolina State University, she worked as an electrical engineer at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. There, she contributed to science instruments on multiple NASA missions. Around this time, she served as a research associate for the U.S. Antarctic Program. Later, as an engineer at the Applied Physics Laboratory, she worked on missions including NASA's Juno spacecraft, which is currently orbiting Jupiter. She was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013. In her expedition to the ISS in 2019, she was part of the first all-female spacewalk in history, and also set the record for the longest continuous stay in space for a woman. Artemis II crew in space The Artemis II crew – (clockwise from left) Mission Specialist Christina Koch, Mission Specialist Jeremy Hansen, Commander Reid Wiseman, and Pilot Victor Glover in the Orion capsule on their way back from the Moon.Image: NASAVictor Glover was born in Pomona, California. He earned his bachelors degree in general engineering from California Polytechnic State University, then became a test pilot for the U.S. Navy, where he was given the callsign "Ike" — short for "I know everything." While serving in the Navy, he earned three Master's degrees (in flight test engineering, systems engineering, and military operational art and science) from Air University and the Naval Postgraduate School. Glover was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013. In his expedition to the ISS in 2020, Glover became the first African American crewmember to live long-term on the space station, as opposed to staying for a brief period as Shuttle or ISS assembly crew did.Jeremy Hansen, From London, Ontario, earned his bachelors in space science and master's degree in physics from the Royal Military College. He served as a pilot in the Canadian Air Force and was selected by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) as an astronaut in 2009. He has also served as CAPCOM, the Capsule Communicator, between Mission Control and the ISS. Christina Koch views Earth from Orion NASA astronaut and Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch looks at Earth from the window of the Orion spacecraft on its way to the Moon during the Artemis II mission. At the time, Christina was already farther away than any woman has ever been from our planet.Image: NASAThe next mission will be Artemis III, a crewed test where Orion will dock with a lunar lander in low-Earth orbit. After that, Artemis IV intends to mark the first crewed Moon landing mission since the Apollo era. NASA is aiming to conduct this roughly 30-day mission to land astronauts on the lunar south pole by 2028. Artemis IV will use the SLS rocket to launch the Orion capsule into orbit around the Moon. Once there, two of the crew’s four astronauts (not yet chosen) will descend to the lunar surface on another spacecraft, possibly SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System. Those two astronauts will spend about a week near the lunar south pole. They will explore the Moon's surface and perform science experiments before returning to lunar orbit to join the rest of their crew for the journey back to Earth. What the Artemis II astronauts did During the mission, the Artemis II crew tested Orion’s various capabilities in deep space. That includes life-support and environmental systems, manual piloting and proximity operations, and communications and navigation systems. The crew also contributed to studies of human physiology, sleep, motion, and other biological responses to space travel. For example, the AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) project used organ-on-a-chip devices to study the effects of increased radiation and microgravity on human health. While in the vicinity of the Moon, the crew also made geological observations that could help scientists refine planning for the Artemis III mission. Orion, the Moon, and Earth A camera on one of Orion's solar arrays captured this image of the spacecraft, the Moon, and Earth in the distance.Image: NASAWhy are we going back to the Moon?Although humans have been to the Moon before, we’ve spent only about 12 days there total. In such a short time, we have accomplished just a small fraction of the science that awaits us. Although robotic missions have explored the Moon since the Apollo era, it’s still worth sending astronauts back. Humans can do science more quickly, flexibly, and intuitively than robots alone, especially when exploring complex terrain and trying to select meaningful samples. The Moon also serves as a testing ground for technologies and skills that are needed for future deep-space missions, including eventual human trips to Mars.Related pages SAVING NASA ScienceYour donation powers our advocacy when it matters most.
